en: The Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa Sūtra, Scroll One; also titled the *Sarvabuddhacaryā-praveśajñānavairocanagarbha-nirdeśa Sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñāyaśas of India during the Zhou Dynasty of the Yuwen clan.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling at the sublime Mahāmālāya [mountain].

On the summit of the mountain, at the edge of a great grove and lotus pond where the Great Mantra-holding Deities dwell—a place inaccessible to ordinary men and the abode of those who have attained the supreme path—he was together with one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus. All of them were mahā-śrāvakas who had completed what was to be done and had transcended the stage of all ordinary beings. Their names were:
the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, along with such other great śrāvakas.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were great bodhisattvas who had attained all the samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and practices of bodhisattvas, and who had all already dwelled in the various bodhisattva stages. Their names were as follows:

The noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Upakāramati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dṛḍhamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samāhitamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anantamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samyaksamāhitamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśuddhamati, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānamati—each of these and all others like them have already received their predictions in their respective Buddha-fields for the sake of turning the wheel of Dharma toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, there were supreme and most excellent devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, along with mantra-holding spirits, non-humans, and others—possessing various forms, celestial crowns, and garments, and holding weapons, banners, and parasols—as well as hosts of ghosts, spirits, and sages, all of whom came and sat together in assembly, desiring to hear the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a multitude as vast as the great ocean, preceding and following him. He preached the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is subtle and elegant, and it fully expounds the pure Brahma-faring in detail.
At that time, within the great city of Laṅkā, there was a rākṣasa king named Vīviṣaṇa who ruled over it.

Then, King Vīviṣaṇa of Laṅkā heard that the Buddha was now dwelling on the summit of the exquisite Mahāmalaya mountain, at the edge of a flower pond in the Great Garden (Mahāranya), in the abode of the great mantra-holding deities—a place where humans cannot travel and which is most conducive to attaining the Way—and that he was manifesting the holy life (brahmacarya) for twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the King of Laṅkā, Vibiśana, immediately gave rise to this thought:
"The name of the Tathāgata is rare in the world; it is like the udumbara flower, which one may hear mentioned only once in countless ages, let alone encountering the Buddha himself."

During this time, for immeasurable and incalculable eons, I have not been able to hear the Dharma; it is like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log. Within this, for the Buddhas and their Dharma, or for those who enter the Buddha’s realm and realize the Buddha-way—such matters are even more exceedingly difficult.

If I were to take with me many precious jewels, as well as strings of pearls, immeasurable incense and flowers, powdered incense and ointments, flower crowns and robes, jeweled banners, flags, and canopies, along with silk streamers, music, and songs of praise, and go together with my retinue to the place where the Buddha is; having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, I would offer these various articles of worship to the Tathāgata, desiring to inquire about the True Dharma so that he might grant me the fulfillment of this life.
Then the Lankā King Viviṣaṇa proclaimed to all the hosts of rākṣasas:

"All of you, with one mind and in harmony, take up abundant and excellent gold, silver, maṇi jewels, *karketana*, lapis lazuli, coral, agate, pearls, necklaces, and red pearls; prepare various exquisite and immeasurable incense and flowers, and perform music and songs of praise. We must proceed to the place of the Buddha, the Dharma King who is most supreme in the three realms, the unsurpassed mass of merit endowed with all marks, the omniscient vision, the unsurpassed field of merit. Let us go toward him, bearing these offerings to present as worship."

"Why is this? Because throughout countless eons, it is difficult to encounter a Buddha appearing in the world, difficult to see a Buddha, difficult to be free from the eight difficulties, and difficult to hear of the Three Jewels.
Having formed this thought, at that time King Vipaśyin Laṅkā addressed the assembly with these verses:
“After immeasurable and incalculable eons, a Buddha finally appears in the world;
yet, wishing to escape the eight difficulties, one must pass through further immeasurable ages and hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas before encountering the World-Honored One.”
Just as the udumbara flower appears only after incalculable time,
so too do beings pass through the hells and the animal realm, and the most painful path of hungry ghosts;
wandering among the six destinies, they revolve like a chariot wheel.
May these classes of sentient beings be freed from all the perils of the eight difficulties;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Lamp of the World appears,
illuminated by the sun of wisdom, able to shatter the blindness of ignorance.
"Follow me to that place, To make offerings to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
He teaches among gods, humans, and the world; By making offerings, one obtains great fruit.

At that time, after King Vipaśyin Laṅkā had spoken this verse, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great nets of light were emitted from the midst of the sky, illuminating the entire great city of Laṅkā.
Having been illuminated, Viviṣaṇa and the entire host of rākṣasas all leaped for joy.
At that time, from within that great mass of blazing light, there issued forth verses on the profound characteristics of phenomena:
"All dharmas are fundamentally quiescent, empty, and without self; Sentient beings cannot be found in the beginning, middle, or end."
Like illusions, dreams, bubbles, mirages, Mist, lightning, foam, and circles of fire— The dharmas of worldly convention are all not real;
The world appears through the roots of ignorance and craving.
In true contemplation, there is neither craving nor ignorance; All dharmas are like space: pure and ineffable.

At that time, when King Vibiṣaṇa of Laṅkā had heard these verses on the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) issued forth from within that net of light, he immediately attained the profound patience regarding the non-self of dharmas (anātma-dharma-kṣānti).
Among that host of rākṣasas, some attained such patience, some gave rise to the bodhicitta, some gave rise to the patience of conformity (ānulomikī-kṣānti), and some attained direct vision.
At that time, the King of Laṅkā, Vibiśana, having attained clarity and freedom from doubt regarding the Buddha-dharma, donned the firm armor of bodhi and further made this vow,
speaking in verse: "The devas, humans, and asuras, All the Brahmā kings and celestial hosts—
Such a supreme and most wondrous Dharma They have never before perceived or realized."
I shall attain this Dharma in the future, Possessing all unimpeded wisdom;
I will realize the Way of the Buddha in this world, Liberating immeasurable billions of sentient beings.
I shall expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas, the most supreme, untainted Eightfold Noble Path,
so that the boundless wisdom I have cultivated may adorn my body with the thirty-two marks of excellence.
If one diligently practices virtuous conduct, And fulfills the practices of the Buddha’s merits,
Benefiting sentient beings and liberating them from fear, Upholding all virtues to extinguish the dust of existence,
With a face like the sun and moon of pure radiance, One shall attain Buddhahood within the triple world.

At that time, the King of Laṅkā, Viviṣaṇa, attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Immediately, in accordance with his intention, there appeared by thought alone all manner of exquisite flowers, incense, unguents, powdered incense, floral crowns, robes, jeweled banners, pennants, parasols, *maṇi* gems bound with silk ribbons, and pearl necklaces. Various musical instruments were played, and the sounds of clapping hands and songs of praise filled the air as they extolled the Tathāgata’s merits, marks, and signs of excellence.

Carrying these various articles of offering, together with their retinue, they proceeded through the air like a king of geese toward the place where the Buddha was; having reached the Buddha’s presence, they descended from the sky.

Then the Lankā King Viviṣaṇa, together with his retinue, turned toward the Buddha with palms joined; he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One one hundred times, and having finished his prostrations, he circumambulated the Buddha three times, even up to a thousand times.
Then the Lankā King Vibiṣaṇa immediately prostrated himself before the Buddha with his five limbs touching the ground, like a felled tree, and further spoke these words:

"Homage to the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the supreme Dharma-body adorned with immeasurable merit, the Lion among Men, and the most eminent in the three realms."
Having spoken these words, he immediately rose and joined his palms, reciting a verse in praise before the World-Honored One:
"In billions of past lives, you perfected your practice with diligence; Through difficult and painful austerities, you sought awakening.
You gave food, drink, clothing, and vehicles, And bestowed billions of the seven treasures upon beggars."
Throughout inconceivable eons, without regret or stinginess, he relinquished his kingdom, villages, ministers, and subjects;
the royal palace with its magnificent and abundant treasures—all that is difficult to give away over billions of eons, he was able to renounce.
Formerly known as Prince Sudāna, he gave away his wife and children in the mountain forests;
first he sacrificed his own body to save a tigress about to give birth, then he cut the flesh from his own limbs to rescue a destitute dove,
and gouged out his eyes to bestow them upon a blind Brahmin— throughout those births, he harbored no resentment.
Giving one’s head as a cause for seeking Bodhi, the mind is always joyful toward those who ask.
To protect the precepts and maintain long-term purity, one does not violate the noble conduct and accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One does not take life or steal the property of others; always following the Brahma-conduct, one is free from envy in the world.
Abstaining from drinking alcohol and false speech, protecting all sentient beings as one's own body;
having never in the past engaged in double-tongued talk or other evil words, nor harbored anger or uttered frivolous speech.
The World-Honored One is free from deviance and ever-tamed; he causes no affliction or offense to sentient beings before him.
His merit is as he intends and he is free from false views; he makes offerings to the Triple Gem with an unbreakable mind.
Having left the home life, stainless and having abandoned the five desires, he followed the Buddha’s precepts and practiced for liberation;
previously, he cultivated patience and endured all sufferings—slander, defamation, and harsh reproach.
All the various pains he suffered in the past were endured without resentment for the sake of sentient beings;
even if someone were to harbor murderous malice toward the Buddha, he would regard them with a heart of loving-kindness as if they were his own child.
The Buddha was born into the world to constantly practice patience, liberating hundreds of millions of suffering sentient beings.
When the Tathāgata sought the Way in the past, he was a great seer named Kṣānti (Patience).
While in that very life, his body was cut and mangled; enduring the pain, he harbored no thought of malice toward the king.
For the sake of that king and his consort, he expounded the White Dharma to bring them joy.
Through constant diligence for inconceivable billions of kalpas, he eliminated indolence, wrong views, and narrow-mindedness;
he was able to endure all former ascetic practices and, through vast diligence, awakened to Bodhi.
Walking in meditation, they neither sleep nor grow weary; They honor and make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
Always acting in accordance with the needs of sentient beings, They cultivate and perfect the unsurpassed Dharma of Buddhahood.
In the past, he practiced meditative concentration to subdue the mind;

having mastered the four dhyānas and the formless attainments, he possessed the power of samādhi, mindfulness, and the five supernormal faculties. Having fulfilled his ancient practices, he attained untainted dhyāna.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is full and untainted; he knows that all phenomena are like illusions and entirely false.
There is no self, no sentient being, no life-force, and no person; they are entangled in the net of afflictions and driven by karma.
The four types of afflictions in the desire realm are impure, yet the realm of sentient beings' afflictions is fundamentally pure;
once one knows that the essence of sentient beings is truly pure, they attain the six pāramitās in their entirety.
Whoever can explain this wisdom and skillful means, diligently seeking the inexhaustible mass of Buddha-blessings, and who,
having developed the three supreme karmas toward the Tathāgata, shall attain Buddhahood in a future life— to that one I prostrate.

At that time, after the King of Laṅkā, Vibiṣaṇa, had spoken these verses, he further honored, revered, and fully served the Tathāgata—with immeasurable varieties of the most exquisite incense, flowers, powdered incense, ointments, floral crowns, robes, precious banners, pennants, and canopies—and with music and song; he made offerings to the Buddha as well as to the assembly of śrāvakas and great bodhisattvas.
The host of rākṣasas did likewise, initiating offerings in accordance with the Dharma that were pleasing to the Buddha’s mind.
At that time, the King of Laṅkā, Viviṣaṇa, having completed his offerings, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now have a doubt and wish to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for me.”
Having spoken these words,
the Buddha addressed King Laṅkā, saying: "King Laṅkā!"
“I shall always grant you permission to ask the Buddha about whatever you doubt; according to your inclination, I will provide an explanation to bring joy to your mind.
At that time, having received this permission, King Laṅkā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“World-Honored One, regarding ‘sentient beings,
sentient beings,’ for what reason is the name ‘sentient beings’ used?
The Buddha said:
“Lakṣaṇasamudgata!

Regarding ‘sentient beings, sentient beings,’ they are called sentient beings because of the aggregation of various conditions; that is to say, they are born from the causes and conditions of earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases.”

Furthermore, "sentient beings" are like a bundle of bamboo; they receive retribution due to conditions of karma, and they obtain fruits due to conditions of karma. The self, the person, the sentient being, the life-span, the nurtured, the aggregate, the knower, the seer, the doer, the toucher, and the feeler—these are called sentient beings.
The Laṅkā King Viviṣaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!
What is that sentient being fundamentally based upon?”
“Upon what does it abide?
What serves as its cause?
The Buddha said:
“Lokendra-rāja! These sentient beings have ignorance as their root, abide by depending on craving, and take karma as their cause.
Lokendra-rāja Viviṣaṇa said:
“World-Honored One,
how many kinds of karma are there?
The Buddha said:
“Karma is of three kinds. What are these three?
They are bodily, verbal, and mental karma. Furthermore, there are three characteristics: pure, impure, and neither pure nor impure.”
Then the Lankā King Viviṣaṇa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that sentient beings relinquish this lifespan and receive that lifespan; how do they relinquish this old body and receive a new body?”
The Buddha said: “Lokendra-rāja!

When sentient beings have cast off this body, the power of the winds of karma blows the consciousness away; they experience the fruits of the karma they themselves have created—whether it be wholesome, unwholesome, or neither wholesome nor unwholesome. As sentient beings perform such karmic actions, they receive a new body in that very place, whether by birth from an egg, moisture, womb, or transformation. All of these are produced by the winds of karma, yet karma itself does not know what it has created; each receives its own retribution.”
“O King of Laṅkā!
Sentient beings are just like this: they relinquish this body and life to receive that new body.
The King of Laṅkā said:
“World-Honored One!
When sentient beings have relinquished this body and life but have not yet received another body, where does consciousness abide during that interval?
The Buddha said:
"Lakṣaṇa-rāja! What do you think?
When a seed in a field reaches the stage of sprouting, does the sprout arise only after the seed has first perished?"
"Does the sprout first emerge and then the seed perish?
Or does the sprout emerge at the very moment the seed perishes?
King Vīviṣaṇa replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“King of Laṅkā!
What is the meaning of this?
King of Laṅkā replied:
“World-Honored One!
When that seed perishes, the sprout immediately arises; it is not that the seed perishes first and then the sprout arises, nor is it that the sprout arises first and then the seed perishes.”
The Buddha said: “So it is,
King of Laṅkā!
It is not that the preceding consciousness ceases first and the subsequent consciousness only then arises.
O King of Laṅkā!
Nor is it that the preceding consciousness arises first and the subsequent consciousness only then ceases.
O King of Laṅkā!
Only when the subsequent consciousness ceases does the preceding consciousness arise.
O King of Laṅkā!
Just as a centipede first places its forefeet down and then follows with its hind feet, such that the bending and extending of its body occurs without interruption—
just so it is, O King of Laṅkā!
“When this consciousness perceives the place of birth before it and has clearly discerned it, the consciousness immediately causes itself to transfer and take refuge there, without any interruption.
King Vipaśyin Laṅkā said:
“World-Honored One!”
"If this is so, is there no intermediate state (antarābhava)?
The Buddha said,
"King of Laṅkā!..."

One type of sentient being is born from an egg; having cast off this body, they enter into an egg, where their consciousness is seized by the winds of karma. Remaining within the egg, they are dull and unconscious; only when the shell has fully formed do they become aware, at which point one should know that the egg has already matured.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of beings born from eggs;
while they have not yet matured, they do not perceive or understand.
Why is this so? It is because of the power of karma,
O King of Laṅkā!

Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose power of merit is pure and profound, who become sons in the family of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); while they are in the womb, they are not defiled by the womb, nor do they dwell together with the impurities of the womb, nor are they contaminated by them.
O King of Laṅkā!

The sons born to that Cakravartin king are mostly born by transformation; even those who are born from a womb, the embryo is already fully formed upon first entering the womb, and as soon as they emerge from birth, they break through the membranes and leave the body.
“Lakṣaṇa King!
For these reasons and conditions, I say that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava).
Then, the Lakṣaṇa King Vipiśana said:
“World-Honored One!
To what extent is the consciousness of sentient beings?
And of what color is it?”
The Buddha said:
"King of Laṅkā!
The consciousness of sentient beings is boundlessly great; it is without color, without marks, and invisible. It is unimpeded, formless, and has no fixed location; it is ineffable."
Viviṣaṇa said: “World-Honored One!

Since the characteristic of consciousness is thus boundless and vast, formless, signless, invisible, unimpeded, shapeless, without a fixed location, and ineffable, would it not be a state of annihilation?”
The Buddha said:
"Lokendra-rāja! I shall now question you; answer as you see fit, and I will explain it for you."
"O King of Laṅkā!
It is like a great king who, while sitting at ease surrounded by court ladies within his palace or upon a high tower, puts on various garments and diverse ornaments."

At that time, the great grove’s *aśoka* trees were adorned with various kinds of flowers, exquisite and magnificent. In that garden, there were gentle, soft breezes or swift winds that blew through those *aśoka* trees of the grove; when the fragrance of the many flowers reached the king's location, did the king perceive it?
Viviṣaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have smelled this fragrance.”
The Buddha said,
“Lokendra-rāja! When you smell this fragrance, do you discern and know it?”
The king said,
“World-Honored One!
I am able to know it.”
The Buddha said:
“Lokendra-rāja! As for this fragrance of the flowers that you say you perceive, do you see it as large or small?”
"What color would it definitely be? King Laṅkā said, "No."
World-Honored One!

Why is this? This characteristic of fragrance is without color and without manifestation; it is unimpeded and signless; it has no fixed location and is inexpressible. Therefore, its large or small form and color cannot be seen.
The Buddha said, "King of Laṅkā! What do you think?
If one does not perceive the magnitude or smallness of that fragrance, is it not a state of non-interruption?"
Viviṣaṇa said: “No, World-Honored One.”
"Why is this? If these various fragrances were of the nature of cessation, no one would be able to smell them.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, O King of Laṅkā! The characteristics of consciousness are likewise; you should view them in this way."
O King of Laṅkā!
If the characteristics of consciousness were severed, then birth and death would not be known.
Thus it is, O King of Laṅkā!
The characteristics of consciousness are pure; they are merely obscured by adventitious afflictions, such as ignorance, craving, habitual tendencies, and karma.
O King of Laṅkā!
It is like the realm of pure space, which is defiled only by four kinds of adventitious dust.
What are these four?
They are smoke, clouds, dust, and mist,
O King of Laṅkā!

The characteristics of consciousness are thus: because it is fundamentally pure, it is boundless, ungraspable, and free from the defilement of form; it is merely obscured and defiled by adventitious afflictions.
Why is this so? O King of Laṅkā!

When one observes correctly, no sentient being is apprehended; there is no self, no sentient being, no life-span, no nourisher, no person, no category of sentient beings, no knower, no seer, no feeler, no experiencer, and no hearer, nor even form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
O King of Laṅkā!
When one observes correctly, there is nothing that can be apprehended through conceptual discrimination. O King of Laṅkā!
All dharmas are a mere conjunction; they possess no intrinsic nature.
Although you have attained this true nature of sentient beings, do not abandon this wilderness of birth and existence.
What is meant by "attaining the true nature of sentient beings"?
It refers to attaining that which is of the same nature as great wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Sentient beings revolve according to the power of their own karma, Failing to attain the supreme path of the Eightfold Noble Ones.
If they leave all karma behind and realize the outflow-free state, They will practice the unsurpassed way to benefit sentient beings.”
Then Viviṣaṇa said: “World-Honored One!

There are immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, within this dense forest and ocean of the three realms—those who have reached the other shore, those who desire to reach it, those who have realized the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, those who have realized the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, and also those who have already realized the sameness of the Great Unsurpassed Wisdom. Furthermore, in future ages, there will be immeasurable, boundless, incalculable, and asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, even more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, who shall each enter nirvāṇa by means of these respective vehicles of the Three Vehicles; yet the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
I know it thus, and a sense of weary disenchantment arises in my mind.
The Buddha said:
“Lakṣaṇasamudgata-rāja!
Do not conceive a sense of weariness or aversion toward this life. Why is that?
Because the realms of all sentient beings cannot be exhausted from beginning to end, so it is with the realm of empty space and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, O King of Laṅkā, the realms of all sentient beings are ineffable; by this one knows they neither increase nor decrease.

Thus, within this ocean of conditioned existence—the dense forest of the three realms—those who have already crossed over and those who wish to cross over do not cause the realm of sentient beings to increase or decrease.
O King of Laṅkā!

For example, the realm of space neither increases nor decreases; it has no beginning, no end, and no middle. Therefore, space cannot be apprehended; it pervades all places, being unobstructed, free from sorrow, without activity, and without conceptualization.
"Even so, even so, Lord of Laṅkā!
Within the realm of sentient beings, one cannot find a beginning, middle, or end upon seeking them.
Lord of Laṅkā!"
Only that which has already attained the commonality of the noble Dharma is called the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings; yet the conditioned path is neither exhausted nor extinguished.
O King of Laṅkā!
Nor is there a path to liberation apart from that. Why?
Because the nature of the realm of sentient beings is such; therefore, it has no beginning, no middle, and no end.
Viviṣaṇa again asked the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of the ocean of conditioned activities of sentient beings?”
The Buddha said:
"King of Laṅkā!
The ocean of conditioned activities of sentient beings is like the great ocean."
He asked the Buddha again:
"World-Honored One!
To what else is the Dharma of all Buddhas similar?"
The Buddha said:
"Lokendra-rāja!
The Dharma of all Buddhas is like a ship."
He asked the Buddha again:
"World-Honored One,
what is the dharma for receiving full ordination by a renunciant bhikṣu like?"
The Buddha said, “King Laṅkā!
A bhikṣu who has received full ordination is like a merchant who boards a ship for the purpose of trade.”
He asked the Buddha again:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said, regarding those who rely on the Buddha’s precepts and laws, fully practicing them without any violation—what are they like?”
The Buddha said:

"Lakṣaṇa-rāja! One who maintains the precepts, exerts diligence, receives the Dharma, and is content with what they have, is like a person engaged in trade who has successfully completed their journey by means of a sturdy ship."
"If there were one who could practice the precepts as taught by the Buddha, without breaking or violating them, and fulfill them completely, it would be just the same.
He then asked the Buddha again:
"World-Honored One!"
“Lokendra, what else is a spiritual friend like?
The Buddha said: “Lokendra!”
"A spiritual friend is like a boatman.
He then asked the Buddha again,
"World-Honored One!"
“Lokendra, to what else is the diligent practice of the Eightfold Noble Path similar?
The Buddha said: “Lokendra!”
"One who diligently practices the Eightfold Noble Path is like a ship being blown by a true, swift wind.
Viśeṣaṇa again asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
“Lokendra, what are meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), samādhi, and the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) like?
The Buddha said: “Lokendra!”
"The supernormal powers and samādhis are like a land of jewels.
Vviṣaṇa again asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
“Lokendra, what are the seven factors of enlightenment further like?
The Buddha said: “Lokendra!”
“The seven factors of enlightenment are like seven kinds of precious gems.
He then asked the Buddha again,
“World-Honored One!”
“Lokavidhvamsana King, what is it like for one who has attained the seven factors of enlightenment and realized the Mahāyāna Samatā?
The Buddha said:
“Lokavidhvamsana King!”

Those who attain the seven factors of enlightenment and realize the Mahāyāna Samatā are like those who obtain the nature of the seven kinds of jewels, becoming immensely wealthy with goods and treasures that satisfy their every wish. Excellent, excellent is the one who has gone forth! Within my Dharma, they realize the unimpeded, unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Observing the suffering of all realms of existence, The suffering of oneself and the suffering of sentient beings,
And having relinquished the bonds of all existences, One goes forth within my Dharma."
"He shall be named a Son of the Buddha, possessing the greatest virtue among the assembly;
by practicing with diligent effort according to the Dharma, he shall become a World-Honored One.
At that time, Vviṣaṇa again asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who, having gone forth within the Buddha-dharma, are unable to maintain the precepts—whether they violate the precepts, break the precepts by engaging in lustful conduct, or cast off their dharma robes, renounce the precepts, and return to lay life;”
“World-Honored One!
To what kind of person is such a foolish man comparable?
The Buddha said:

"Lakṣaṇa-rāja! If there are sentient beings who, having gone forth within my Dharma, receive the precepts and yet commit various transgressions, these deluded people will mostly fall into the evil realms, just as a merchant at sea whose ship is wrecked perishes in the water."
Viviṣaṇa said: “World-Honored One!

If there are those who break the precepts, violate the discipline, or engage in lustful conduct, yet claim, ‘I practice diligence and the holy life,’ or those who cast aside their Dharma robes, abandon the precepts, and return to secular life—when such persons die and pass away, if they are reborn in a good destination, what would that be like?”
The Buddha said:

"It is like a person seeking a livelihood who, upon the great ocean, finds their ship destroyed and sinks into the water; some may find a plank, some may find a corpse, and some may float by their own strength."
O King of Laṅkā!
Those merchants who obtained a plank were blown by the force of the wind until they reached an island.
Those who clung to a corpse were gradually pushed to the other shore by the waves of the sea.
Why is this? It is because the nature of the great ocean is not to harbor corpses.
If one can float across by one's own strength and reach wherever one desires, it is due to the compassionate salvation of the sea deity.
"So it is, so it is, King of Laṅkā!

If those who have gone forth in my Dharma cannot rely upon the precepts and maintain them according to the Dharma, yet cast off the monastic rules and put on secular clothing, they may still be reborn in a good realm—whether by having attained right faith through me, or because their inner nature is pure, or even if they have broken the precepts, they constantly practice compassion or possess diligence."
"Therefore, O King of Laṅkā!
Even those who have broken the precepts or returned to secular life may, by means of my Dharma, be reborn in auspicious realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In past lives throughout boundless billions of births, I have committed many sinful deeds;
now I confess them openly and shall not create them again. By extinguishing them so they do not increase, I am purified."
Then Viviṣaṇa again asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are there?"
The Buddha said:
"King Laṅkā! There are thirty-seven factors that assist the realization of enlightenment."
What are called the thirty-seven factors?
They are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
“Lokendra-rāja!
These are called the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening.
He then asked the Buddha again:
“World-Honored One!
How many gates of liberation are there?
The Buddha said:
“Lokendra-rāja! There are three gates of liberation.
What are the three?
"These are what are called emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He then asked the Buddha again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What dharma should one keep in mind?
The Buddha said,
"One should keep in mind weariness with existence, cessation, and entry into nirvana."
He again asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of remedial dharmas (pratipakṣa) are there in total?"
The Buddha said:
"Lokendra-rāja! To speak in brief, there are three kinds of remedies."
What are these three? They are:

the contemplation of impurity for those with a mind of lustful desire, the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion for those with a mind of hatred, and the contemplation of dependent origination for those with a mind of delusion; these are called the three methods of remedial counteraction.
He asked the Buddha again:
"World-Honored One,
how many skillful abilities must one keep in mind and maintain?"
The Buddha said,

“King of Laṅkā! One who must practice mindfulness and upholding should be skillful in knowing the aggregates (skandhas), skillful in knowing the elements (dhātus), skillful in knowing the sense bases (āyatanas), and skillful in knowing the expedient means (upāya).”
He asked the Buddha again:
"World-Honored One!
What contemplation should one practice?"
The Buddha said:
"Lokendra-rāja! You must contemplate the profound twelve links of dependent origination and the realization of the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths."

At that time, the King of Laṅkā, Vipaśyin, again circumambulated the World-Honored One three times. He scattered various flowers made of the seven precious gems over the Buddha; having finished scattering them, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and, in wonder and praise for the Tathāgata, spoke these verses:
“What are the various noble practices of a bodhisattva, By which they give rise to a mind of diligence to benefit the world?”
Through generosity, morality, patience, and diligence, He resolved his supreme mind upon Bodhi;
While seeking that untainted wisdom, He gathered and transformed many billions of sentient beings.
Adorned with myriad jewels and free from all defilement, He attained Buddhahood within a most exquisite land.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the King of Laṅkā, Vipaśyin, saying:
“Excellent, excellent,
King of Laṅkā!”
That you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this matter—listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you.
King of Laṅkā!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva must constantly practice the six pāramitās and never give rise to malicious thoughts toward any sentient being.
Lokagarbharāja!

When a bodhisattva practices such dharmas, they neither diminish nor decrease; they constantly increase in all Buddha-dharmas, and are neither defiled by nor attached to worldly dharmas. They gather in and transform immeasurable sentient beings, purify the buddha-fields of the Tathāgatas, and further fully attain the sameness of great wisdom, remaining unobstructed and unhindered within the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the King of Laṅkā, Vibiśana, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should one practice?”
"How can one abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? The Buddha said: "Abandon arrogance, conceit, and envy;

constantly practice the four kinds of pure brahmacarya; with joy, always act with correctness and truth for the sake of all sentient beings. You must abandon killing, stealing, false speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, harsh words, drinking alcohol, and sexual misconduct. Do not allow yourself to momentarily forget the mind of bodhi. With a joyful intent, diligently practice the six pāramitās; whatever you do, always do it for the peace and happiness of sentient beings. Keep your mind constantly tranquil amidst conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Desiring to cross the ocean of existence which is full of many terrors, you should correctly contemplate the sentient beings of the three realms so that they may attain liberation."
"Furthermore, Lord of Laṅkā!
If you wish to seek awakening (bodhi), you must understand it in this way: what is called 'awakening' is merely a name and a verbal expression; it is simply designated as 'awakening. "
Why is this so? O King of Laṅkā!
There is no such thing as bodhi; bodhi is rootless, bodhi is non-abiding, and bodhi is stainless.
This is bodhi; bodhi is free from dust; bodhi is without self; bodhi is ungraspable;
bodhi is formless; bodhi is shapeless; bodhi is without "this"; bodhi is without "that";
bodhi is without sorrow; bodhi is without affliction; bodhi is without...
Attachment is bodhi; non-defilement is bodhi; boundlessness is bodhi; the unconditioned is bodhi;
the absence of turbidity is bodhi; that which has transcended all faculties is bodhi;
the elimination of all recollections and conceptualizations is bodhi; that which has transcended all conditioned activities is bodhi; it is bottomless.
This awakening is difficult to know; this awakening is profound; this awakening is without letters;
this awakening is without marks; this awakening is quiescent; this awakening is pure;
this awakening is unsurpassed; this awakening is beyond analogy; this awakening is without seeking.
Enlightenment is the severance [of delusions]; enlightenment is non-destruction; enlightenment is non-fracture;
enlightenment is the absence of discursive thought; enlightenment is the absence of substantial entities; enlightenment is the unconditioned; enlightenment is the absence of views;
enlightenment is the absence of harm; enlightenment is the absence of ignorance; enlightenment is the absence of outflows.
Eternity is bodhi; space is bodhi; the peerless is bodhi;
the ineffable is bodhi.
O King of Laṅkā!
O King of Laṅkā! For one who seeks awakening, if they do not seek dharmas, that is seeking awakening.
Why is this? O King of Laṅkā!
If there is no attachment, one can realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, by being without the mark of a self, the mark of a sentient being, the mark of a life-span, the mark of a person, the mark of a nourisher, the mark of a multitude, the mark of an agent, the mark of an experiencer, the mark of a knower, and the mark of a viewer, one can then realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If one does not perceive the characteristics of conventional truth, one will not be attached to dharmas, nor attached to the aggregates (skandhas) or the elements (dhātus), and so on, up to not being attached to the Buddhas or Bodhisattvas; only then can one realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this so? O King of Laṅkā!
That which is free from all attachment is itself bodhi.
If one does not cling to things, does not cling to permanence, and does not cling to annihilation, one will realize and perfect awakening in a future life. Why is this so?
"King of Laṅkā!
Because all dharmas are extinguished at their posterior limit.
Then, King Vipiśana of Laṅkā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How can one come to know all conventional dharmas?
The Buddha said:
“Lakṣaṇa-rāja!

Know that all phenomena of worldly convention are like illusions, like transformations, like dreams, like mirages, like the moon reflected in water, and like the city of the Gandharvas. All phenomena of worldly convention should be known in this way, realized in this way, and contemplated in this way.”

At that time, the King of Laṅkā, Vipaśyin, immediately attained a bodhisattva samādhi called "The Wisdom-Characteristic of the Light of the Dharma Unequaled," and he attained a dhāraṇī called "All Skillful Sounds."
Having attained such immeasurable and boundless samādhis and dhāraṇīs, the King of Laṅkā, Vibiśana, then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Now that I have attained this samādhi-dhāraṇī, I am awakened to and know all phenomena of worldly truth.
The Buddha said, "King Laṅkā!"
"How does one become aware of it? Vviṣaṇa said,
"World-Honored One!"

“World-Honored One! All phenomena of worldly convention are like a dream, like an illusion, like an echo, like a swift mountain stream, like the moon in water, like flowers blown by the wind in the sky, like autumn clouds arising, like the radiance of a jewel, like the flame of a lamp, like dew upon a flower, like a city of the Gandharvas, like bubbles on the water, like a rainbow, and like a mirage.”
"I have already realized that all phenomena of the conventional truth are currently impermanent.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of various wondrously colored rays of light—namely, colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, crystal, and gold—which universally illuminated immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable Buddha-fields. Having shone everywhere, they returned and re-entered the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, spoke in verse, asking:
"The Buddha’s supreme and wondrous virtue is not without cause; He has released a pure net of radiant light.
Whom does your mind now intend to awaken with this exquisite realization? Emitting a hundredfold net of light, I pray the Buddha will speak."
The Buddha addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:

“Do you see this King Vipaśyin Laṅkā standing before me with palms joined, using these vast offerings to honor me, the assembly of śrāvakas, and the assembly of bodhisattvas; and by virtue of this merit, has he resolved his mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
Maudgalyāyana said:
“World-Honored One,
I see it.”
“World-Honored One!
I have seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Maudgalyāyana!

This King Vipaśyin Laṅkā will, from this time forth until he has made offerings to and served hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, thereafter—his body endowed with the fundamental power of merit—be reborn in a world named Padmāvatī. There dwells a World-Honored One, named Padmaguṇalakṣaṇasvaravega-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there, wandering and preaching the Dharma.”
The lifespan of that Buddha-Tathāgata is immeasurable, and his world is pure.

This King Laṅkā, Vvi-vi-śa-na, was born by transformation in that land; having been born there, he immediately attained the Bodhisattva stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), and thus proceeded until he attained the tenth Bodhisattva stage. After the passing of immeasurable kalpas, he will later be born in this Sahā world and shall attain Buddhahood, known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named *Suvicitra-nirghoṣa-suvarṇateja-suvimalaprabhābhāsa-guṇaratnacchatravyūha-śīrṣa-vairocana-rāja*.
This is his final birth.
That world is named Electric Jewel Crown; it is devoid of mountains, hills, pits, ravines, precipices, slopes, earth, stones, and filth, and there is no female form or the evil realms.

Moreover, that buddha-field is more pure and sublime than the present buddha-field of the Tathāgata Amitābha; it is filled with hosts of bodhisattvas, its eon is named "Excellently Contemplated Radiance," and the lifespan of that Buddha, the Tathāgata, is immeasurable.
"Maudgalyāyana!
For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha smiles.

At that time, when King Vipaśyan Laṅkā received the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, for the sake of the Dharma, he was filled with joy and exultation; his entire body trembled as he flew up into the air to the height of seven tala trees. From mid-air, he spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are empty like dreams; pure and non-existent, they are like space.
Both self and non-self are entirely absent; I know them to be like illusions and like flashes of lightning."
Sentient beings arise and perish within existence; though one seeks diligently for a single dharma, it cannot be found.
In the beginning, middle, and end, there is nothing at all; the same is true for the lives of those whom they nourish and raise.
Sentient beings receive retribution according to their karma, Transmigrating through the realms of existence without rest;
If one practices such bodhisattva conduct, One will realize that the essence of all phenomena is empty.

At that time, after the King of Laṅkā, Viviśana, had spoken these verses, he descended from the air, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and having completed the three circumambulations, sat to one side through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.

At that time, among the assembly gathered on the ocean, there were some devas, nāgas, asuras, and others who realized the Dharma and attained the fruits [of the path]; some yakṣas and rākṣasas who gave rise to the bodhicitta; some kiṃnaras and mahoragas who attained freedom from doubt regarding all Buddha-dharmas; and some garuḍas, gandharvas, and mantra-deities who attained dhāraṇīs, realized the Dharma, attained the fruits [of the path], and became non-retrogressive regarding all phenomena.

Immediately, the great earth shook, and natural radiance filled the Buddha-field, illuminating everywhere even between the Great and Small Iron Ring Mountains. All sufferings in the various evil realms were entirely eliminated. From the sky above, celestial flowers rained down, and the sounds of celestial drums beating and shrilling resounded; furthermore, garments unfurled and rolled up in the air, and such various inconceivable phenomena spontaneously appeared.
Then the Lankā King Vibiṣaṇa surveyed his own assembly and addressed them thus:
"All of you, come together in harmony toward the World-Honored One; give rise to a heart of reverence and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Then those immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rākṣasas gathered together and, joining their palms toward the Buddha, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have assembled and come together; from this day forward, we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and resolve to attain bodhicitta.”
"World-Honored One!
From this day forward, we shall practice the path of the Mahāyāna; may the Tathāgata bear witness to this.
World-Honored One!"

"In future ages, we shall attain perfect enlightenment within this Sahā world-system; we shall certainly sever all evil karma to become Unsurpassed Honored Ones for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings."
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
If you are able to resolve upon bodhicitta, you should practice four kinds of wholesome dharmas.”
All those who practice wholesome deeds and cultivate these four dharmas shall not forget that bodhicitta. What are the four?

First, to ensure that all vows and practices are neither contravened nor lost; second, to constantly maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; third, to make offerings to the Triple Gem three times each day, continuing without interruption throughout the day and night; and fourth, not to aspire for the fruits of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
“This is for you to be fully endowed with these four dharmas so as not to forget that bodhicitta.
At that time, Sāgara, the Dragon King, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

What roots of goodness did the Lankā King Vviṣaṇa cultivate in the past, such that he was able to provide such extensive offerings to the Buddha and the countless assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; and having completed these offerings, how did he resolve his mind upon awakening (bodhicitta), and having resolved his mind upon awakening, how did he realize non-retrogression and receive the prediction of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi)?
Having spoken these words,
the Buddha addressed the Dragon King Sāgara, saying: "Dragon King!

That Tathāgata has likewise been reborn in this Sahā world during the age of the five corruptions; that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, expounds and distinguishes the Dharma of the Three Vehicles among sentient beings.
"O Dragon King!

At that time, that Tathāgata was also dwelling upon this summit of Mount Malaya, preaching the Dharma in the midst of a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus who were great śrāvakas, as well as immeasurable devas, nāgas, and non-human beings."
"O Dragon King!

At that time, there was a rākṣasa youth named Vibiṣaṇaka who also resided in this great city of Laṅkā. His appearance was fierce and formidable, with a massive chest and great strength; his nature was cruel and violent, and his face and features were loathsome and ugly. He subsisted solely on flesh and blood, and his mouth and fangs were terrifying."
"O Dragon King!
At that time, the rākṣasa youth Vibiśāka, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling upon the summit of Mount Malaya, immediately thought to himself:
'I do not wish for this śramaṇa and his assembly of bhikṣus to reside upon the summit of Mount Malaya.'"

Why is this? If that śramaṇa were dwelling on the summit of Mount Malaya, I would not be able to seize the various creatures of the great ocean, nor would there be any sentient beings to be slain; staying here now, I shall remain in constant hunger.
"O Dragon King!
At that time, the rākṣasa youth Vipiśāka immediately addressed his host of rākṣasas, saying:

'You who possess great strength, you should come quickly; don firm armor and each take up swords, pestles, mallets, crossbows, axes, halberds, bows, arrows, spears, shields, as well as vajras, battle-wheels, lances, and so forth—rigorously bearing such various weapons.'"
Why is this? I must now expel that śramaṇa and his assembly from my realm, causing them to abandon the place where I dwell.
"O Dragon King!

At that time, the rākṣasa youth Vibiśaṇa, accompanied by a host of rākṣasas wearing fine and sturdy armor, each holding various weapons of distinct colors, flew through the air toward the Tathāgata Jñānanimitta-dhvaja born of Great Compassion."
Having arrived there, he stood suspended in mid-air and addressed the World-Honored One and his retinue, saying:
"Begone, begone, śramaṇa! I have no need for you to dwell upon this mountain peak; do not cause me again to kill you, śramaṇa, and your followers."
"O Dragon King!
At that time, the Tathāgata Wisdom-Phase-Banner Born of Great Compassion manifested supernormal powers.

Having manifested these powers, the rākṣasa youth Vibiśaka and his retinue each saw themselves bound by fivefold fetters; they further saw iron nets spread out in the ten directions, and though they wished to flee, there was no way, and they stood there paralyzed with terror."
“O Dragon King!
At that time, the rākṣasa youth Vibiśaka and the host of rākṣasas were seized with alarm and fear, and they immediately thought:
‘Where shall we go now?’”
To whom shall we go for refuge?
To whom shall we turn for rescue?
Who will deliver us from this peril?
"O Dragon King!

At that time, within the assembly of that Buddha, there was a mantra-king named Samādhi-gambhīra-pūrṇa-guṇa-tejas, who had been a close friend since his youth with the rākṣasa youth Vibiṣāṅga; he was seated among the assembly of that World-Honored One."
"O Dragon King!
At that time, the Dharani-king Śrīgarbha-guṇa-tejo-dhara, who abides in right concentration, spoke to the rākṣasa youth Vipiśāka, saying:
'Good friend!'"

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach and transform humans and devas; they have attained immeasurable dharmas of merit and are uniquely honored throughout the three realms. They are jewels among sentient beings, possessing the practice of great compassion.
"You, my good friend, and you hosts of rākṣasas, you may take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
By taking refuge in the Three Jewels and generating the bodhicitta, all your bonds shall be immediately liberated."
Having spoken these words, O Dragon King!

At that time, through the power of the conversion of the Mantra-holding Deity-King of Profound and Perfect Merit and Sustenance (Viniścaya-gambhīra-pūrṇa-guṇa-tejo-dhara), and by the supernatural power of the Buddha, the rākṣasa youth Viviṣāgara and the assembly of rākṣasas immediately joined their palms together and spoke these words:

“Homage to the one whose body is adorned with boundless merit! Homage to the Supreme Greatly Compassionate Awakened One! From this day forward, we and you shall take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. We shall constantly practice taking refuge in the Triple Gem and resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"O Dragon King!

When the rākṣasa youth Vibiśaka and the entire assembly of rākṣasas had uttered these words, all their bonds were immediately released; they came from the sky toward the Tathāgata Great Compassion-Arisen Wisdom-Characteristic Banner King and, having reached that Blessed One, circumambulated him three times."

Then the rākṣasa youth Vibiṣaṇa and the entire host of rākṣasas simultaneously prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and requested his forgiveness from that Tathāgata; having finished their request for forgiveness, they each returned to their own abodes.
“Nāga King!
What do you think?
You should know that the rākṣasa youth Vibiṣaṇa of that time and world—was he anyone else? It was none other than me.”
The present King Vibiṣaṇa of Laṅkā is he.
As for that host of rākṣasas in that world at that time, they were no other group; it was this very host of rākṣasas belonging to King Vibiṣaṇa of Laṅkā who were they.
"O Dragon King!
What do you think?

That King of the Mantra-holding Spirits named Samādhi-gambhīra-pūrṇa-guṇa-tejo-dhara who appeared in that world at that time was no other person; he was none else than the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sāgaramati-gambhīra-dhāraṇī-vaśitā-jñānābhijña."

Having spoken these words, this trichiliocosm immediately shook, like a ship upon the great ocean swaying with the waves. Among the various classes of sentient beings, none were seen to be terrified or harmed; instead, all attained peace, security, and happiness, and all sentient beings maintained the ten virtuous actions.

At that time, this Sahā Buddha-field was cleared of high mountains, Mount Sumeru, the great oceans, kingdoms, villages, mountain forests, islands, dark mountains, caves, dense thickets, gardens, ponds, rivers, springs, marshes, plateaus, mounds, pits, ravines, cliffs, ridges, rocky walls, sandy wastes, thorns, mud, excrement, and all foul, filthy, and loathsome things—except for Jambūnada gold.

A great light shone universally throughout this trichiliocosm, illuminating all the darkness within every great and small Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*), as well as all places where the sun and moon do not shine; that radiance pervaded everywhere, eclipsing the sun and moon, let alone all other lights.
At that time, all shadows vanished, and the sufferings of all beings in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts were extinguished.

Immediately, all gods and humans in this Sahā world who were afflicted by distress attained peace and experienced happiness. Among those sentient beings, the hungry received food, the thirsty received drink, the naked received clothing, the poor received treasures, the blind saw forms, the deaf heard sounds, and the mute were able to speak; those with impaired faculties all became complete, and those imprisoned in dungeons were universally liberated.
